An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. The subject counting process and at-risk process are $N_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\le t,\ \delta_i=1\}$ and $Y_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge t\}$.
The endpoint convention makes $Y_i$ left-continuous at $U_i$: a subject is still at risk at the observed time, including a tied event and censoring time. Set $N_n=\sum_{i=1}^nN_i$ and $Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $dN_n$ be the finite counting measure of observed events on $[0,\infty)$, with atom $\Delta N_n(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\ \delta_i=1\}$ at each $u\ge0$; in particular, $\Delta N_n(0)=N_n(0)$. Tied failures at $u$ contribute their full count and censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $dN_n(u)$.

For $t\ge0$, the **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)=\int_{[0,t]}\frac{\mathbf 1\{Y_n(u)>0\}}{Y_n(u)}\,dN_n(u)$, where the integrand is defined to be zero when $Y_n(u)=0$. The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.
Each product is finite and a factor is zero if every subject at risk fails at that time. The target survival function is $S(t)=P(T>t)$. If $T$ has density $f$, $S$ is positive on the horizon, and $\lambda=f/S$, the continuous cumulative hazard is $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du=-\log S(t)$.

These inclusive endpoint formulas reduce to the usual $(0,t]$ formulas whenever $\Delta N_n(0)=0$. If $T$ has finite support $0\le a_1<\cdots<a_m$, write $q_j=P(T=a_j\mid T\ge a_j)$; the corresponding discrete cumulative hazard is $\Lambda_d(t)=\sum_{a_j\le t}q_j$. Under IID sampling, independent censoring, and positive risk probability at the support points, the Nelson–Aalen increments estimate these $q_j$; in general this discrete cumulative hazard is not $-\log S(t)$.

A baseline event is included at $u=0$; if it occurs then $N_i(0)=1$, so a model contract requiring $N_i(0)=0$ must exclude this case.

An empty event product is $1$, and an empty Greenwood event sum is $0$.

On a horizon where every event contribution has $Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)>0$, the **Greenwood variance estimate** is $\widehat V_G(t)=\widehat S_n(t)^2\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)\{Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)\}}$.
Greenwood's formula is used as a first-order asymptotic variance estimate when the sampling and censoring assumptions justify that approximation; the formula alone asserts no asymptotic result and is not an exact finite-sample variance identity. It is undefined when a contributing denominator is zero.

For each fixed $t$, $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)$ and $\widehat S_n(t)$ are statistics of the observed sample in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Greenwood's formula is a measurable function on the measurable subset $D_n(t)$ of the observed sample space $([0,\infty)\times\{0,1\})^n$ where every contributing denominator is positive. Its **zero extension** $\widehat V_G^\circ(t)$, equal to $\widehat V_G(t)$ on $D_n(t)$ and $0$ elsewhere, is a statistic on the whole observed sample space. This extension assigns no Greenwood variance interpretation outside $D_n(t)$.

To verify measurability, scan indices $i=1,\ldots,n$ and include only the first event observation at each distinct time in $[0,t]$; each inclusion condition uses finitely many Borel equalities and inequalities among the observed $U_i$ and $\delta_i$. Risk and event counts are finite Borel sums. The finitely many positive-denominator tests make $D_n(t)$ measurable; evaluating divisions only on their positive-denominator branches makes the sums, products, and zero extension Borel measurable.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Both CDFs are right-continuous, so their supremum error over $\mathbb R$ is the supremum over rational $x$; over $[-t,0]$ it is the supremum over $(\mathbb Q\cap[-t,0))\cup\{0\}$ (with $\{0\}$ alone when $t=0$). Thus both suprema are measurable. Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$. Choose the finitely many distinct quantiles $x_k=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge k\varepsilon\}$ for $1\le k<1/\varepsilon$, together with $x_0=-\infty$ and $x_{m+1}=+\infty$, where $m$ is the number of distinct finite cutpoints. At each finite cutpoint, both $F_n(x_j)$ and $F_n(x_j-)$ converge in probability to their expectations by Chebyshev's inequality applied to the IID indicators $\mathbf 1\{V_i\le x_j\}$ and $\mathbf 1\{V_i<x_j\}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. The subject counting process and at-risk process are $N_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\le t,\ \delta_i=1\}$ and $Y_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge t\}$.
The endpoint convention makes $Y_i$ left-continuous at $U_i$: a subject is still at risk at the observed time, including a tied event and censoring time. Set $N_n=\sum_{i=1}^nN_i$ and $Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $dN_n$ be the finite counting measure of observed events on $[0,\infty)$, with atom $\Delta N_n(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\ \delta_i=1\}$ at each $u\ge0$; in particular, $\Delta N_n(0)=N_n(0)$. Tied failures at $u$ contribute their full count and censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $dN_n(u)$.

For $t\ge0$, the **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)=\int_{[0,t]}\frac{\mathbf 1\{Y_n(u)>0\}}{Y_n(u)}\,dN_n(u)$, where the integrand is defined to be zero when $Y_n(u)=0$. The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.
Each product is finite and a factor is zero if every subject at risk fails at that time. The target survival function is $S(t)=P(T>t)$. If $T$ has density $f$, $S$ is positive on the horizon, and $\lambda=f/S$, the continuous cumulative hazard is $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du=-\log S(t)$.

These inclusive endpoint formulas reduce to the usual $(0,t]$ formulas whenever $\Delta N_n(0)=0$. If $T$ has finite support $0\le a_1<\cdots<a_m$, write $q_j=P(T=a_j\mid T\ge a_j)$; the corresponding discrete cumulative hazard is $\Lambda_d(t)=\sum_{a_j\le t}q_j$. Under IID sampling, independent censoring, and positive risk probability at the support points, the Nelson–Aalen increments estimate these $q_j$; in general this discrete cumulative hazard is not $-\log S(t)$.

A baseline event is included at $u=0$; if it occurs then $N_i(0)=1$, so a model contract requiring $N_i(0)=0$ must exclude this case.

An empty event product is $1$, and an empty Greenwood event sum is $0$.

On a horizon where every event contribution has $Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)>0$, the **Greenwood variance estimate** is $\widehat V_G(t)=\widehat S_n(t)^2\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)\{Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)\}}$.
Greenwood's formula is used as a first-order asymptotic variance estimate when the sampling and censoring assumptions justify that approximation; the formula alone asserts no asymptotic result and is not an exact finite-sample variance identity. It is undefined when a contributing denominator is zero.

For each fixed $t$, $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)$ and $\widehat S_n(t)$ are statistics of the observed sample in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Greenwood's formula is a measurable function on the measurable subset $D_n(t)$ of the observed sample space $([0,\infty)\times\{0,1\})^n$ where every contributing denominator is positive. Its **zero extension** $\widehat V_G^\circ(t)$, equal to $\widehat V_G(t)$ on $D_n(t)$ and $0$ elsewhere, is a statistic on the whole observed sample space. This extension assigns no Greenwood variance interpretation outside $D_n(t)$.

To verify measurability, scan indices $i=1,\ldots,n$ and include only the first event observation at each distinct time in $[0,t]$; each inclusion condition uses finitely many Borel equalities and inequalities among the observed $U_i$ and $\delta_i$. Risk and event counts are finite Borel sums. The finitely many positive-denominator tests make $D_n(t)$ measurable; evaluating divisions only on their positive-denominator branches makes the sums, products, and zero extension Borel measurable.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Under the finite-horizon contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], the optional
quadratic variation of $M=N-A$ is $[M]_t=N_t$, its continuous predictable
bracket is $\langle M\rangle_t=A_t$, its self-cross predictable bracket is
$\langle M,M\rangle_t=A_t$, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale on $[0,T]$.

For the compensator contract on $[0,T]$, let $H$ be a predictable real
process with
$$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty.$$
When the elementary integrals of a sequence of bounded predictable step
processes converging to $H$ in this norm converge in $L^2(P)$, denote the
resulting $L^2(P)$ class at time $t$ by
$$\int_0^t H_s\,dM_s.$$
The definition is conditional on existence of the limit. The L²-extension
theorem below proves existence for every such predictable $H$, independence
from the approximating sequence, the martingale property, and the isometry.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the conditional-expectation and
$L^2$-completion interfaces used by that theorem.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

Let $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ be IID real-valued observed times. For every positive integer $n$, define $\bar Y_n(u)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge u\}$ and $s_0(u)=P(U_i\ge u)$. For every finite $t\ge0$,
$$\sup_{0\le u\le t}|\bar Y_n(u)-s_0(u)|\to_P0,\qquad E\left[\sup_{0\le u\le t}|\bar Y_n(u)-s_0(u)|^2\right]\to0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $(\mathcal O,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, and let $O_1,O_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be a measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued estimator based on $O_1,\ldots,O_n$ for a fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $\phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable, $E_P\phi=0$, and $E_P\|\phi\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $\Sigma=E_P[\phi\phi^T]$. Assume the separately established expansion, with remainder $r_n$ on the sample probability space,

$$\hat\theta_n-\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(O_i)+r_n,\qquad r_n=o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$

The remainder notation means $\sqrt n\,r_n\to_P0$, as in [[def-asymptotically-linear-estimator-and-influence-function]]. Thus $\phi$ is the estimator influence function in the asymptotically linear sense: the theorem assumes the expansion and does not establish it. The covariance may be singular, including zero.

Let $d,k\ge1$, let $r_n>0$ be deterministic with $r_n\to\infty$, and let $T_n$ be $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with target $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $Z_n=r_n(T_n-\theta)\Rightarrow Z$ for an $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector $Z$. All vector norms below are Euclidean.

If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ is Borel and there is a linear map $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=Ah+\rho_1(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_1(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow AZ.$$

If, in addition, $A=0$ and there is a continuous symmetric bilinear map $H:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=\frac12H[h,h]+\rho_2(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_2(h)\|}{\|h\|^2}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n^2\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow \frac12H[Z,Z].$$
For scalar-valued $g$, $H$ is the usual Hessian bilinear form. The second-order premise is a pointwise Peano expansion; continuous second derivatives on a neighborhood are not required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Independence within a subject gives $s_0(u)=P(T_i\ge u,C_i\ge u)=S(u)G(u)$. On $[0,t]$, $s_0(u)\ge c:=S(t)G(t)>0$. Since $S$ is absolutely continuous and $S'(u)=-f(u)=-\lambda(u)S(u)$ almost everywhere, integration of $(\log S)'=-\lambda$ gives $\Lambda(t)=-\log S(t)$. The assumed integral makes $\sigma^2(t)$ finite and also gives $\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du<\infty$.

For each finite $n$, event times have no ties in $(0,t]$ almost surely: for $i\ne j$, subject independence and the absolutely continuous law on $[0,t]$ give $P(T_i=T_j\le t)=0$, and there are finitely many pairs. Thus $N_n=\sum_iN_i$ is a simple counting process. Set $Y_n=\sum_iY_i$, $A_n=\sum_iA_i=\int_0^{\cdot}Y_n(u)\lambda(u)\,du$, and $M_n=\sum_iM_i=N_n-A_n$. Finite sums preserve the martingale property and square integrability; [F4] gives $E[A_n(t)]=\sum_iE[A_i(t)]<\infty$. The process $J_n=\mathbf 1\{Y_n>0\}$ is predictable, and so is $\eta_n=Y_n\lambda$ by [F11]; both meet [F4]'s domain, with $A_n=\int_0^{\cdot}J_n(u)\eta_n(u)\,du$. Hence the pooled process also satisfies the finite-horizon contract. By [F5], its predictable bracket is $A_n$.

We will identify the completed integrals with pathwise finite-variation integrals for every bounded predictable integrand $H$ used below. The paths of $Y_i$ and $\bar Y_n$ are left-continuous on $(0,t]$, and $s_0(u)=P(U_i\ge u)$ is left-continuous there by continuity of probabilities along decreasing events. Consequently $s_0^{-1}$, the floored reciprocal $b_n$, its difference $H_n$, and the floored product reciprocal $q_n$ below all have bounded left-continuous paths, with a deterministic bound for each fixed $n$. On deterministic partitions with mesh tending to zero, take the left-step approximants $H^{(m)}(u)=H(t_j)$ on $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$ and set their time-zero value to zero. They are elementary predictable integrands, converge pointwise to $H$ at every $u>0$, and retain the bound. For any subject or pooled contract, [F13] for the finite compensator measure $E\,dA$ gives $E\int_0^t|H^{(m)}-H|^2dA\to0$, and [F7] gives convergence of their elementary integrals to the completed integral in $L^2(P)$. The paths of $M=N-A$ have finite variation; [F13] applied pathwise to its finite variation measure gives convergence of the same elementary sums to $\int_{(0,t]}H\,dN-\int_0^tH\,dA$. Uniqueness of limits in probability identifies these two limits almost surely at the fixed time. The time-zero convention is immaterial because $N_0=A_0=0$ and $A$ is continuous. This proves the pathwise identities needed below without assuming a general semimartingale integration theorem.

Write $\bar Y_n=Y_n/n$. By [F8], $E[\sup_{u\le t}|\bar Y_n(u)-s_0(u)|^2]\to0$. Let $b_n(u)=1/\max(\bar Y_n(u),c/2)$ and $H_n(u)=b_n(u)-1/s_0(u)$. These are bounded predictable processes: $\bar Y_n$ is predictable by [F4], and Borel transformations preserve predictability by [F11]. The reciprocal map with floor $c/2$ is $4/c^2$-Lipschitz, so $E[\sup_{u\le t}|H_n(u)|^2]\to0$.

The energy of $H_n$ for $M_n$ is finite because $H_n$ is bounded and $E[A_n(t)]<\infty$. Applying [F7] to the pooled contract gives $E|n^{-1/2}\int_0^tH_n\,dM_n|^2=n^{-1}E\int_0^tH_n^2\,dA_n=E\int_0^tH_n^2\bar Y_n\lambda\,du\le (\int_0^t\lambda\,du)E[\sup_{u\le t}|H_n(u)|^2]\to0$. Thus this stochastic-integral remainder is $o_P(1)$. On the event $E_n=\{\sup_{u\le t}|\bar Y_n(u)-s_0(u)|<c/2\}$, whose probability tends to one by [F8], $Y_n(u)>0$ throughout and $b_n=1/\bar Y_n$. By the pathwise identification in step 2.1, $d\bar N_n=\bar Y_n\lambda\,du+d\bar M_n$ gives there $\sqrt n(\widehat\Lambda_n-\Lambda)=n^{-1/2}\int_0^t b_n\,dM_n$. For each bounded predictable step integrand, the finite-sum definition in [F6] makes the integral against $M_n=\sum_iM_i$ equal to the sum of the subject integrals. Approximate $s_0^{-1}$ in the pooled compensator energy by such steps; [F7] gives L² convergence, and $dA_i\le dA_n$ lets the same approximants converge for each of the finitely many subjects. Since $s_0^{-1}$ is a deterministic Borel time function, it is predictable by [F11]. Passing the finite-sum identity to these L² limits yields $\sqrt n(\widehat\Lambda_n-\Lambda)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\int_0^t s_0^{-1}\,dM_i+o_P(1)$.

For one subject, step 2.1 identifies the integral in step 3.1 as $\phi_i^\Lambda(t)=\mathbf 1\{\delta_i=1,U_i\le t\}/s_0(U_i)-\int_0^{U_i\wedge t}\lambda(u)/s_0(u)\,du$, so it is a measurable function of $(T_i,C_i)$. It has mean zero by the martingale property and, by [F7] and Tonelli [F12], variance $E\int_0^t s_0(u)^{-2}\,dA_i(u)=\int_0^t s_0(u)^{-2}E[Y_i(u)]\lambda(u)\,du=\int_0^t\lambda(u)/s_0(u)\,du=\sigma^2(t)$. The integrand is nonnegative and product-measurable because $Y_i$ is predictable and $s_0^{-2}\lambda$ is a deterministic Borel function. Hence these influence variables are IID and square-integrable. The normalized IID sum is bounded in probability by its fixed second moment, so step 3.1 gives a separately established expansion with $o_P(n^{-1/2})$ remainder. Applying [F9] proves $\sqrt n(\widehat\Lambda_n-\Lambda)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2(t))$.

On $E_n$, for all sufficiently large $n$, every event jump has size $x=1/Y_n(u)\le2/(nc)\le1/2$. For $0\le x\le1/2$, the power series for $-\log(1-x)-x$ gives $|\log(1-x)+x|\le x^2$. There are at most $n$ event jumps, so $|\log\widehat S_n(t)+\widehat\Lambda_n(t)|\le4/(nc^2)$. Consequently $\sqrt n\{\widehat S_n-e^{-\widehat\Lambda_n}\}\to_P0$. Step 4.1 also gives $\widehat\Lambda_n-\Lambda=O_P(n^{-1/2})$; Taylor's formula for $e^{-x}$ on $[0,\infty)$ then yields $\sqrt n(\widehat S_n-S)=-S(t)n^{-1/2}\sum_i\phi_i^\Lambda(t)+o_P(1)$. Taking $g(x)=e^{-x}$ and derivative $g'(\Lambda)=-S(t)$ in [F10] transfers the terminal normal limit, giving $N(0,S(t)^2\sigma^2(t))$.

For sufficiently large $n$, define the bounded predictable $q_n(u)=[\max(\bar Y_n(u),c/2)\max(\bar Y_n(u)-1/n,c/4)]^{-1}$. On $E_n$, $\Delta N_n(u)=1$ at event times and $q_n(u)=1/[\bar Y_n(u)(\bar Y_n(u)-1/n)]$, so $n\sum_{u\le t}\Delta N_n(u)/[Y_n(u)(Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u))]=\int_0^tq_n\,d\bar N_n$. The uniform convergence in [F8] implies $q_n\bar Y_n\to1/s_0$ uniformly in probability, while $q_n$ is uniformly bounded. Using step 2.1, decompose $\int q_n\,d\bar N_n=\int q_n\bar Y_n\lambda\,du+n^{-1}\int q_n\,dM_n$. The first term tends to $\sigma^2(t)$ by boundedness and $\int\lambda<\infty$; by [F3]–[F4] the second has second moment at most $n^{-1}(8/c^2)^2E[A_1(t)]$, which tends to zero. Therefore the scaled Greenwood sum tends to $\sigma^2(t)$, and $\widehat S_n(t)^2\to_P S(t)^2$ by step 5.1. Since $P(E_n)\to1$ and Greenwood's formula is defined on $E_n$ for large $n$, the zero extension agrees with the formula on an event whose probability tends to one. It follows that $n\widehat V_G^\circ(t)\to_P S(t)^2\sigma^2(t)$, which equals $\operatorname{Var}(\phi_i^S(t))$ by step 4.1. This is a first-order variance estimate, not a finite-sample identity.

citations.quote:
An **event time** is a measurable real-valued map $T$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. A **covariate** is a measurable map $Z$ into a specified standard-Borel space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal B)$, where standard Borel means measurably isomorphic to a Polish space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]). A **censoring or inspection time** is a measurable real-valued map $C$ with values in $[0,\infty)$. When conditional laws are used, they are probability kernels $K_T(z,\cdot)$ and $K_C(z,\cdot)$ in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. They are part of the specified model; their existence for real-valued targets and factorization through standard-Borel $Z$ follow under [[def-axiom-of-choice]] from [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]].

The notation $T\perp\!\!\!\perp C\mid\sigma(Z)$ has the meaning in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: for bounded measurable $a,b$, $\mathbb E[a(T)b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]=\mathbb E[a(T)\mid\sigma(Z)]\mathbb E[b(C)\mid\sigma(Z)]$ almost surely. It is a model assumption about the conditional observation law, not a consequence of adjusting for $Z$ and not an empirical conclusion.

Under **right censoring**, the recorded pair is $U=\min(T,C)$ and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$. Thus $\delta=1$ records an event at $U=T$, including a tie, while $\delta=0$ records censoring at $U=C$ and implies $T>C$. **Left censoring** at a known threshold $L$ records only $T\le L$. **Interval censoring** at known endpoints $L<R$ records $L<T\le R$. **Current-status observation** at an inspection time $C$ records only $\delta_C=1\{T\le C\}$.

**Left truncation**, also called delayed entry at $L$, selects a unit into the sample only when $T>L$; observation begins after that selection. **Right truncation** at $R$ selects a unit only when $T<R$. These are selection rules before the observed sample is formed, whereas censoring coarsens an event time after sampling. The strict and weak inequalities in these definitions fix the endpoint conventions. A random observation endpoint is called noninformative here only when it is fixed by design or is generated independently of $T$ conditional on the stated covariates under a parameter-distinct law; otherwise its joint observation law must be modeled.

For a positive integer sample size $n$, let $(T_i,C_i)$, $1\le i\le n$, be event and censoring times with right-censored observations $(U_i,\delta_i)$ as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]], so $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. The subject counting process and at-risk process are $N_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\le t,\ \delta_i=1\}$ and $Y_i(t)=\mathbf 1\{U_i\ge t\}$.
The endpoint convention makes $Y_i$ left-continuous at $U_i$: a subject is still at risk at the observed time, including a tied event and censoring time. Set $N_n=\sum_{i=1}^nN_i$ and $Y_n=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Let $dN_n$ be the finite counting measure of observed events on $[0,\infty)$, with atom $\Delta N_n(u):=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i=u,\ \delta_i=1\}$ at each $u\ge0$; in particular, $\Delta N_n(0)=N_n(0)$. Tied failures at $u$ contribute their full count and censorings at $u$ do not contribute to $dN_n(u)$.

For $t\ge0$, the **Nelson–Aalen estimator** is $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)=\int_{[0,t]}\frac{\mathbf 1\{Y_n(u)>0\}}{Y_n(u)}\,dN_n(u)$, where the integrand is defined to be zero when $Y_n(u)=0$. The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.
Each product is finite and a factor is zero if every subject at risk fails at that time. The target survival function is $S(t)=P(T>t)$. If $T$ has density $f$, $S$ is positive on the horizon, and $\lambda=f/S$, the continuous cumulative hazard is $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du=-\log S(t)$.

These inclusive endpoint formulas reduce to the usual $(0,t]$ formulas whenever $\Delta N_n(0)=0$. If $T$ has finite support $0\le a_1<\cdots<a_m$, write $q_j=P(T=a_j\mid T\ge a_j)$; the corresponding discrete cumulative hazard is $\Lambda_d(t)=\sum_{a_j\le t}q_j$. Under IID sampling, independent censoring, and positive risk probability at the support points, the Nelson–Aalen increments estimate these $q_j$; in general this discrete cumulative hazard is not $-\log S(t)$.

A baseline event is included at $u=0$; if it occurs then $N_i(0)=1$, so a model contract requiring $N_i(0)=0$ must exclude this case.

An empty event product is $1$, and an empty Greenwood event sum is $0$.

On a horizon where every event contribution has $Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)>0$, the **Greenwood variance estimate** is $\widehat V_G(t)=\widehat S_n(t)^2\sum_{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)\{Y_n(u)-\Delta N_n(u)\}}$.
Greenwood's formula is used as a first-order asymptotic variance estimate when the sampling and censoring assumptions justify that approximation; the formula alone asserts no asymptotic result and is not an exact finite-sample variance identity. It is undefined when a contributing denominator is zero.

For each fixed $t$, $\widehat\Lambda_n(t)$ and $\widehat S_n(t)$ are statistics of the observed sample in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Greenwood's formula is a measurable function on the measurable subset $D_n(t)$ of the observed sample space $([0,\infty)\times\{0,1\})^n$ where every contributing denominator is positive. Its **zero extension** $\widehat V_G^\circ(t)$, equal to $\widehat V_G(t)$ on $D_n(t)$ and $0$ elsewhere, is a statistic on the whole observed sample space. This extension assigns no Greenwood variance interpretation outside $D_n(t)$.

To verify measurability, scan indices $i=1,\ldots,n$ and include only the first event observation at each distinct time in $[0,t]$; each inclusion condition uses finitely many Borel equalities and inequalities among the observed $U_i$ and $\delta_i$. Risk and event counts are finite Borel sums. The finitely many positive-denominator tests make $D_n(t)$ measurable; evaluating divisions only on their positive-denominator branches makes the sums, products, and zero extension Borel measurable.

derivations.claim: At time $1$, all four subjects are at risk and one fails, so $Y_1=4,d_1=1$. At time $2$, three remain at risk and one fails, so $Y_2=3,d_2=1$. By [F2], $\widehat\Lambda_n(3)=1/4+1/3=7/12$ and $\widehat S_n(3)=(1-1/4)(1-1/3)=1/2$.

Both Greenwood denominators are positive, and [F2] gives $\widehat V_G(3)=\frac14\left(\frac1{4\cdot3}+\frac1{3\cdot2}\right)=1/16$. The two censorings at time $3$ add no event increment, so all three estimates remain at these values after time $3$ if the product and sum are carried forward.

Under either law in [A1], an event time above $3$ produces the same observed record $(U,\delta)=(3,0)$; event times $1$ and $2$ produce $(1,1)$ and $(2,1)$. Thus the entire observed-data law is identical under $P_A$ and $P_B$, while $P_A(T>4.5)=0$ and $P_B(T>4.5)=1/2$. Survival beyond the censoring horizon is therefore not identified by these observations.
